content: Environmental factors and specific settings can influence hemoglobin levels, and adjustments to hemoglobin cutoffs for diagnosing anemia may be necessary in certain contexts: 1. Elevation of Residence: Hemoglobin concentrations are affected by the altitude at which individuals reside. It is recommended to adjust hemoglobin levels when diagnosing anemia to account for the effects of living at higher elevations. A standardized set of adjustments has been proposed for populations living at altitudes below 2500 meters, where the majority of the global population resides. For example, hemoglobin adjustments increase incrementally with elevation, starting at 4 g/L for 500–999 meters and reaching 33 g/L for elevations of 4500–4999 meters. These adjustments are either subtracted from observed hemoglobin levels or added to the anemia cutoff values. 2. Smoking: Adjustments for smoking status are recommended when diagnosing anemia. For instance, smokers with an unknown quantity of cigarettes smoked or those smoking fewer than 10 cigarettes per day require a 3 g/L adjustment, while those smoking 10–19 cigarettes per day require a 5 g/L adjustment, and those smoking more than 20 cigarettes per day require a 6 g/L adjustment. These adjustments are applied by either adding the specified value to the anemia cutoff or subtracting it from the observed hemoglobin level. 3. Infection and Inflammation: Hemoglobin levels are influenced by infections and inflammation, particularly in settings with endemic diseases like malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV. However, it is not recommended to adjust hemoglobin cutoffs for anemia diagnosis based on these factors. Biomarkers such as C-reactive protein and α1-acid glycoprotein are used to adjust iron-related biomarkers but not hemoglobin. Chronic low-grade inflammation, as seen in obesity or non-communicable diseases, can alter iron metabolism and contribute to anemia, but hemoglobin adjustments for these conditions are not advised. Additional indicators are needed to determine the underlying causes and severity of anemia in such cases. 4. Genetic Ancestry, Ethnicity, and Race: Hemoglobin concentrations vary across populations due to genetic differences, but there is insufficient evidence to recommend adjusting hemoglobin cutoffs for anemia diagnosis based on genetic ancestry, ethnicity, or race. For example, Black individuals have been reported to have lower mean hemoglobin levels (approximately 10 g/L lower) compared to White individuals. When diagnosing anemia, it is essential to consider genetic, nutritional, infectious, and social determinants of health relevant to the individual or population. Capillary blood samples (e.g., from finger pricks) show variability compared to venous samples, and adjustments to make them comparable are not currently possible. Quality Control: Accredited instruments, international calibration standards, and proper sample handling are critical for reliable results. Alternative Methods: In settings where automated analyzers are not feasible, approved point-of-care devices calibrated against international standards may be considered. Hemoglobin as a Marker for Iron Interventions Hemoglobin concentration is a simple marker for assessing the impact of iron interventions, such as supplementation or food fortification. However, it only reflects the later stages of iron deficiency (iron deficiency anemia) and may miss earlier stages. Measuring additional biomarkers like ferritin and serum transferrin receptor, along with markers of inflammation, is recommended for a comprehensive assessment of intervention outcomes. Public Health Significance of Anemia The classification of anemia prevalence as a public health concern (mild, moderate, or severe) should remain unchanged until new evidence becomes available. This classification is based on total anemia prevalence across all age groups and is used to guide public health planning and interventions. Moderate and severe anemia are more clearly associated with adverse clinical outcomes, while the implications of mild anemia are less well-defined. Global Context and Recommendations Anemia is a significant global public health issue, particularly affecting women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and children in lowand middle-income countries. Accurate diagnosis and understanding of anemia's causes are essential for effective interventions. The World Health Organization (WHO) aims to reduce anemia prevalence by 50% in women of reproductive age by 2025, as part of its global nutrition targets and sustainable development goals. This requires evidence-based guidelines for measuring hemoglobin and defining anemia, tailored to diverse populations and settings.
